power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Preferences underpin a range of fitness behaviors for many mammals such as foraging, object interactions, and even social relationships.
Despite the ubiquity of domestic dogs in modern culture, the basis for preferences driving their behavior and choices are not well understood.
Past work has found that dogs perceive and respond to certain characteristics of items, specifically an object's familiarity and quality when making choices.

However, in the real world, these characteristics don't exist in isolation, and understanding the interaction between familiarity and valuation as they relate to object choice can provide insight into how dogs make decisions.
We aimed to explore how item familiarity and quality intersect to form dogs' preferences for one food over another in a series of two-alternative forced choice tasks.

Over three studies, dogs (N = 125) were presented with a classic preference test between two items of unequal quality (Study 1), systematic pairings of four items that contrasted familiarity and quality (Study 2), and aggregates of two items of unequal quality (Study 3).
Overall, we found that dogs' choices were driven only by the quality of the food item, and the prior familiarity of the item did not impact choice behavior.
Consumption measures revealed preferences that were not consistently reflected in choices.
Determining what motivates dogs and contributes to their preferences has implications for understanding decision-making at large, as well as for advancing canine science.

text.text: Like other species, dogs regularly make decisions such as what to eat (e.g., a piece of their kibble or mystery food found on a walk) and what to play with (e.g., a kong or a ball).
In making these decisions, it is beneficial to evaluate the characteristics of the objects at hand.
For instance, choosing to eat or interact with a novel item, like a new food found on a walk, carries some degree of risk, but may provide a valuable resource if that is a new delicious food source.

Making quality-based decisions requires integrating multiple characteristics of an object (such as tastiness and novelty), and trading off potential risks (e.g., the likelihood the food will cause illness) with the potential benefits (e.g., discovering a new high-calorie food source), to form a preference and make the resulting choice.
Preferences, which we define here as an underlying, relatively stable assignment of value to one item over another, are driven by the items' features.
Choices, the observable behavior of selecting an item in a given context, can also hinge on other characteristics of the individual or the environment.
Food preferences and choice behavior in social mammals appear to be influenced by several internal and external factors.

Studies with human and nonhuman primates have found that internal forces shaping preferences may include individual differences (e.g., sex or age) and tastes (Drewnowski, 1997), an individual's nutritional needs (Laska et al., 2000; Verspeek & Stevens, 2020), or even early developmental experiences and exposure (Birch, 1999; for a review see Ventura & Worobey, 2013).

text.text: External forces, such as the current social environment or competition (Hopper et al., 2011; Kumpan et al., 2019), resource density (Parrish et al., 2020), conditions of (un)certainty around obtaining the food (Huskisson et al., 2021), the relative value of one food compared to other available options (Freeman et al., 2013; Hopper et al., 2014), or even how much effort it would take to obtain one item over another (Bonnie et al., 2019) can also influence which choices are made.

text.text: Together, this prior work underscores the complex nature of preference formation and how it supports behavior.

In particular, it highlights that choices may not be a straightforward reflection of an item's subjective or relative value for the chooser, but rather a behavior that is strongly influenced by both the context of the choice and the item's characteristics.

The interaction of preferences and choices is particularly relevant to understand for animals that depend on humans for care and wellbeing, such as those housed in zoos or are domestic species used in farming or kept as companions.
Another facet shaping preferences and choice behavior is balancing neophilic and neophobic strategies in food gathering.

A neophilic approach promotes exploration and the discovery of new food sources, while a more cautious approach can buffer against eating potentially harmful foods (i.e., the "omnivore's dilemma"; Milton, 1993).

text.text: Such skills are also highly relevant to domestic dogs, a species that has evolved to thrive on a starch-rich diet similar to humans (Axelsson et al., 2013) but that preferentially select food that is high in protein when it is available (i.e., meat-based foods; Sarkar et al., 2019).

text.text: To date, dogs have received comparatively little attention when it comes to food preferences, even though this is highly relevant for many applied fields where selecting appropriately motivating rewards can enhance learning and inform care standards.

Here, we extend the broader literature on preference formation and novelty-seeking, to examine whether dogs' initial choices track their underlying preferences, or instead reflect more context dependent decision processes.
As a species that is commonly kept as a companion, dogs provide a particularly interesting model for studying how object characteristics influence quality-based choices under variable conditions.
As social, domestic carnivores who have evolved alongside human beings, research with dogs has provided insights into the effects of domestication on decision making.

For example, dogs are sensitive to item quantity (Petrazzini & Wynne, 2016; Ward & Smuts, 2007) but perform more poorly on numerical reasoning tasks than wolves, as evidenced by dogs showing a comparatively weaker preference for the larger quantity of a desirable food (Range et al., 2014), suggesting that domestication may alter item value or item choice strategies.

text.text: Understanding dogs' preferences provides an important context for understanding their cognitive abilities.
This is particularly important because dogs are relied on in a variety of service roles such as guiding visually impaired individuals or alerting to changes in medical status.
Understanding what motivates dogs and how they form preferences can help to advance canine science and improve training for working dogs.
Some features of items are preferentially chosen by dogs over others.
For example, as discussed previously, dogs will choose items based on their quantity.
Dogs also form preferences for items based on the item's qualities.

It may be intuitive to think that a high quality food item (e.g., something rich in fat or with high caloric quality) will be preferred over a low quality item, but this has not been explicitly examined.
Dogs have preferences for foods and make consistent choices based on these preferences (Cameron et al., 2021; Vicars et al., 2014).

However, the majority of dogs either significantly preferred the location with the consistently preferred food reward or showed no preference (Bremhorst et al., 2018).

text.text: Dogs also choose items based on the items' novelty or familiarity.
For instance, given a choice of toys, two of which are familiar and one is new, dogs prefer the novel toy (Kaulfuss & Mills, 2008).

text.text: A preference for new things, known as neophilia, is not unique to dogs.
Neophilia has previously been explored in a variety of species including non-human primates (Kendal et al., 2005) and birds (Heinrich, 1995).

text.text: Neophilia is associated with innovation, and neophilic individuals may be more likely to discover novel solutions to problems and may be able to exploit new resources (Amici et al., 2019).

text.text: However, a preference for novelty comes with risk.
New items may be harmful or dangerous, and acquiring those items may expose the individual to elevated risks of predation or injury.
Individuals who avoid this risk are neophobic.
They display a strong preference for familiar items and rarely interact with new foods or objects.

Critically, preferences for novelty can vary based on context, meaning an individual may be neophilic in one domain (i.e., choosing a novel toy), but be neophobic in another (i.e., choosing a familiar food) (Amici et al., 2019; Kuczaj, 2017).

text.text: While dogs are neophilic when selecting toys, it's not currently known whether they prefer novel items in other domains, such as foods.
In the present research, we examined the role of item value and familiarity in dogs' food preferences and choice behavior.
In Study 1, we tested whether dogs systematically chose high-quality food items in a laboratory setting using a classic, two-alternative forced choice task.

Across four task variations that manipulated the presentation and visual access to the items (in the experimenters' hands, on plates, dropped into cups, or in aggregate inside of jars) dogs were shown two food items of unequal quality and familiarity (hotdog = high value and familiar, versus dried corn kernel = low value and unfamiliar) and allowed to choose one.

In Study 2, we aimed to disassociate item value and item familiarity, two features known to individually impact dogs' choices between food items, to explore how they intersect in dogs' choice of one food over another.

We presented dogs with a total of four distinct food items (high value familiar & unfamiliar; low value familiar & unfamiliar) across six possible pairings, allowing for the exploration of the impact of familiarity and value in isolation, as well as their combined impacts (i.e., if dogs are willing to take a risk on an unfamiliar food when the alternative is of low value).

In Study 3, we explored if a novel choice paradigm would impact dogs' displayed preferences for high quality items, relative to a classic two-alternative forced choice.
Study 1 was conducted in-lab.

In part due to the COVID-19 pandemic, Studies 2 and 3 were conducted via Zoom with a synchronous citizen science design, where dog guardians acted as experimenters with real-time virtual support from a researcher.

text.text: For the first step in our investigation of dogs' choice behavior, we focused on item value in a simple two-alternative forced choice task.

Since prior research suggests that dogs may be integrating diverse dimensions of an item when deciding whether to eat or interact with it, we created a choice scenario between two items that differed in quality or value (i.e., tastiness).
We controlled for other features such as item size, quantity, numerosity aiming to motivate choice behavior supported by dogs' underlying preferences for high quality food items alone.
We predicted that when dogs were offered a choice between two food items, they would select and eat the high quality option more often compared to the low quality option.
Further, we predicted that value would outweigh other aspects of the choice scenario, such as simultaneous or sequential item presentation which might impact the salience of the items.

To test whether dogs integrate item value into their choice behavior when in a lab environment, we tested four types of item presentation that have been commonly used in studies of canine cognition: placing on plates, holding in hands, dropping inside cups, and in aggregate inside of transparent jars.

This study was approved by the [BLINDED] University Animal Care Committee (UACC), guardians gave informed written consent prior to participating, and all procedures were in accordance with university and federal ethics guidelines.
We recruited companion dogs (N = 51) from a large urban area (Female = 25) to participate in-lab at the university.
An additional 11 dogs were excluded from the final analysis for being unwilling to complete all trials in the study (n = 8), or due to experimenter baiting error (n = 3).
None of the dogs had prior experience participating in research and we did not implement any breed or training requirements for inclusion.
Guardians volunteered their time and were compensated for transportation to the lab.
Prior to beginning the study, guardians gave informed written consent for their dog to participate in the activities.
During the study, guardians remained in the room, sitting behind their dog's sightline and out of view of both the handler and dog while the task was in progress (Figure 1).

We truly randomly assigned dogs to participate in a baseline condition (nBaseline = 10), or one of four experimental conditions of the two-alternative choice task (nHands = 10; nPlates = 11; nCups = 10; nJars = 10).
Across all tasks, each dog had a brief acclimation period in the room while off leash, 3-5 minutes of exploration time.

During the task, dogs worked on standard 6-foot leash and were handled by a trained research assistant to ensure they were a consistent distance from the choices on all trials and were stationary, facing the experimenter during the demonstration.

In baseline, we presented dogs with a choice between a white plate with a freeze-dried beef liver treat and a plate with nothing, to confirm that dogs would consistently approach a location with a food item over an empty location (rather than exhibiting random behavior).

We controlled for human enhancement of the search locations during item presentation by simultaneously moving both hands laterally to the search locations and placing the item at one and holding the empty hand above the other.
To motivate a preference-based choice from the dogs in the four experimental conditions, we selected two edible items of similar size but that differed substantially in color and quality.
The high quality items were microwaved beef hotdog slices and the low quality items were dried Peruvian choclo (dried giant white corn kernels).
With similar size items, we controlled for the possibility that dogs made choices based on reward quantity rather than item preference.
The four experimental conditions all involved a choice between these items while presentation of the items was varied systematically.

In the Hands condition, dogs watched the experimenter simultaneously present a single high and low quality item in the palms of her extended hands (arms at 45˚ lateral angle from the median, at dog's head height).
The Plates condition was similar, but items were presented on two 9-inch blue plastic plates that were set on the floor ~0.9m apart (Figure 1).

text.text: Presenting both items simultaneously allowed for equal viewing of the items prior to making a choice.
The experimenter timed item presentation across trials and tasks so that there was a three-second interval between item placement and verbally releasing the dog to make a choice.
In the Cups and Jars conditions, items were presented sequentially, the high or low quality one at a time, in a counterbalanced order across trials.

In the Cups condition, the experimenter placed both cups at the search locations, then showed the dog one item one at a time, before dropping it into a blue plastic cup and repeating the motion with the second item.

In the Jars condition, the experimenter picked up each jar one at a time from the floor and held it out toward the dog to show that it was full of either the high or low quality items, before placing it at one of the search locations and repeating the motion with the second jar.
Sequential presentation allowed the dogs to view each of the items prior to making a choice, then they could approach one jar and receive an item sampled from within.
The cups were blue plastic cups that were 10 cm in diameter at the rim and 12 cm in height.
The jars were clear plastic jars with opaque lids that were 10 cm in diameter and 20 cm in height.
In all conditions, the interval between placement and releasing the dog was three seconds.
We intentionally equalized odor cues across all conditions so that scent could not differentially inform the dogs' choices, allowing us to focus on visual cues.
This approach is consistent with other two alternative forced choice paradigms in canine cognition that control for odor, and effectively removes scent as a quality or location cue.
We amplified the highquality item scent in the environment and rubbed hotdog slices on all stimuli (including the experimenter's hands) before each session.

To help with air movement and cover light background noises that might be distracting to the dog, a small table-top fan was placed at the back of the room and set to a low setting during the test session.
All dogs participated in a brief warm-up after acclimating to the space.
The experimenter sat on the floor facing the dog while the handler brought the dog into a stationary position facing the experimenter, about 1.3 meters distant.
The handler held the dog at the starting position throughout the demonstration until release.
The experimenter drew the dog's attention calling "look" and extending a treat at arms-length in front and around eye-level for the dog.
The experimenter placed the treat on the floor and verbally released the dog to approach and eat the treat.
Dogs that hesitated to approach were encouraged vocally by the experimenter and the actions were repeated until they approached without signs of hesitance or anxiety (typically 2-4 trials).
Following the warm-up, dogs assigned to the experimental condition were introduced to the high quality item (hotdog slice) and low quality item (corn kernel), so that each was familiar.
The same showing and baiting procedure from the warm-up was used, each item was introduced twice (four total trials).
Item introduction began with the high quality item and alternating between the two options, and ended with the low quality item.
This brief item introduction allowed dogs to learn about the items prior to the choice task and establish a similar level of familiarity prior to the choice task.
Dogs assigned to the baseline condition did not have an item introduction and proceeded immediately to test trials following the warm-up.

In all of the test conditions (including baseline), the dog and experimenter were at a distance of 1.3 meters facing one another, the dog was released verbally by the experimenter to make a choice, and was recalled to the starting location by the handler following their choice on each trial (Figure 1).

text.text: To minimize human influence on the dogs' choices during the test, the handler and experimenter did not look or gesture at either of the items or directly to the dog, and were silent apart from the verbal release and recall words.
A brief pause of three seconds occurred between baiting and verbal release, allowing the dog to observe the two options.
Upon making a choice (i.e., touching one of the items or the container that held it), the other option was removed from access to prevent exhaustive searching.
Locations were baited in a counterbalanced order across trials, so that the treat (or the high value item) never appeared in the same location more than twice consecutively.
Dogs completed a total of 10 choice trials.

In the Cups and Jars conditions, where food items were presented sequentially rather than simultaneously, the order of showing high or low quality item first was counterbalanced to control for primacy effects.
Procedure timing and the lateral search locations were consistent across all conditions, including baseline.
Dogs in all conditions completed 10 test trials of the Two-alternative Choice task and were live-coded by the experimenter for their approach and choice on each trial.
Live-coded choice results were confirmed through video coding by a trained research assistant, with 100% agreement.
Choice per trial was coded based on the dog's first touch of the food item or container (cup, plate, jar, or hand) with their muzzle or forepaw.

We scored correct choices as one (defined as touching the high quality item first or, in the case of baseline, the plate with the treat) and incorrect choices as zero (defined as touching the low quality, or empty plate, first).
Choices were summed across trials per dog, to a possible total score out of 10.
Consumption of the item following choice was coded post-hoc from video (for details on consumption coding and results of analyses, see the accompanying Supplemental Information).
We analyzed the data in R (v4.5.3; R Core Team, 2026), all scripts and data are available on OSF following publication.

To understand if dogs, as a group, were above chance at selecting the treat in baseline or the high value item in experimental conditions, we used two-tailed t-tests (α = .05), where chance performance was 5/10 correct trials.

To test the impact of the presentation style on choice behavior, in a series of linear regression models we compared performance in experimental conditions, as well as performance in experiments (pooled) to baseline.

Finally, to explore if dogs increased or decreased in accuracy over trials, we performed mixed logistic regression analyses with accuracy as the dependent variable, a 318 random intercepts per dog, and trials nested within the dog.

When dogs were presented with two visually distinct food items of the same size, one low and one high quality, they chose the high quality item approximately 58% of the time, which, while above chance, is not strong evidence of preference-motivated choice behavior in this context.
In the baseline condition (choosing a treat over nothing) dogs showed a strong tendency to select the treat which suggests that they are not choosing randomly.
However, when tasked with differentiating between two items based on quality, their choices only weakly reflected this preference.
In two of the tasks, item presentation was simultaneous, which may have caused the dogs to split their looking time between the two or even choose one item to fixate on.
In both the Hands and Plates conditions where both items were shown and placed at the same time, dogs' performance did not differ from chance.
In the Cups and Jars conditions, we used a sequential presentation to ensure that dogs had looked at each item prior to making a choice.

While performance was still near chance levels, dogs were selecting the high quality item slightly above the simultaneous presentation conditions, suggesting that perhaps forcing attention to each item could be helpful for decision making.
Looking at the choice data alone, it would be reasonable to infer that dogs do not have a strong preference for hotdog versus dried corn, as they choose the two items at similar rates.
However, this could be mistaking task demands and decision making challenges for a weak preference between the items.

To take a closer look at the possibility that dogs did not have an underlying preference for one item over the other, in follow-up analyses we used data on whether the chosen item was consumed after choice.

We found that on trials where dogs selected the hotdog, the probability that they would eat the item was 99%, while if they had selected dried corn, then the probability dropped to 19.3% (see Supplemental Information for the details of this post-hoc analysis).
This strongly suggests that dogs prefer to eat hotdogs over corn, and that perhaps there are other challenges that prevent this preference from being consistently expressed in their choices.

Such challenges could be due to information gathering strategies that may rely less on vision (i.e., scent detection, and everything in the room smelled like hotdog), or dealing with the demands put on inhibitory control in various problem-solving scenarios (e.g., Bray et al., 2014), or even possibly an evolutionary adaptation for an indiscriminate diet and scavenging behavior.

text.text: Finally, the task itself may not have been an optimal situation for measuring dogs' preferences.
However, one additional possibility is that dogs' preferences for foods are formed from a combination of the item's quality and familiarity.
Specifically, dogs may be assigning value based on how novel the items are, and end up making choices based on a composite quality judgment that integrates multiple features of an item.
None of the dogs in this study had previously been exposed to a Peruvian choclo.
Giant corn kernels may have indeed been low preference, but potentially high novelty food items, with these two criteria in competition.

Even though the item introduction was intended to reduce novelty and put the items on equal footing with regard to familiarity in the task, it is possible that two repetitions were not enough exposure to accomplish this goal.
In contrast to the corn, it is likely that some, but perhaps not all of the dogs had previously encountered hotdogs over the course of their general training.

This opens the possibility that, in addition to individual differences in neophilia that may exist between dogs, the dogs in this study may also have differed in their familiarity with the specific food items, and this could have influenced their choice behavior.
In Study 2, we aimed to explore how dogs make preference-based choices when integrating multiple features of objects, such as item quality and object familiarity.
To address this, we carried out another study directly examining the influence of item familiarity and quality on behavior in a two-alternative choice task.

In Study 2, dogs completed six types of two-alternative forced-choice pairings of four guardian-selected foods: high quality familiar, high quality unfamiliar, low-quality familiar, and low quality unfamiliar.

Across comparisons, dogs' choices could be driven by the quality of the item alone, in which case we would expect that they would choose the high (vs. low) quality items in all pairings where that comparison is present.
We would also expect that when the items did not differ in quality, they would choose between the two at chance levels.

Dogs could also make choices driven by the relative familiarity of the item alone, in which case, we would expect that they would show strong preferences when comparing relatively familiar and unfamiliar items, but when comparing items of equal familiarity we would expect choices at chance levels.
Dogs may also display a ranked preference that is dependent on both factors where, for example, dogs most prefer one item and may rarely choose another item.
Finally, they might not show strong preferences for item quality or familiarity as measured by our choice metric.

text.text: It is also worth noting that our familiarity manipulation concerned dogs' prior familiarity with the foods.
We allowed dogs to sample each food item twice prior to the test trials, so that they could have direct experience of each item's quality.
Therefore, our findings concern the effects of prior or relative familiarity and do not establish how dogs respond to entirely unencountered foods.
Dogs usually consumed their chosen item in Study 2, fully consuming it on 1,738 of 1,807 codable trials (96.2%).
However, as in Study 1, when dogs did not fully consume their chosen item, it was almost always a low quality item (61 of 69 trials, 88.4%).

This suggests that the lower quality item was in fact less preferred, though dogs in Study 2 were more likely to consume the low quality item than in Study 1 (see Supplementary Materials for a summary of item consumption).
This may be because even the low quality foods were selected individually by guardians and sampled before testing to establish that they were edible.
One possible explanation is that task demands contribute to dogs' apparent weak preferences (as measured by choices).
For example, dogs may have a difficult time with impulse control, resulting in choices that are not in line with their true preferences.
Pet dogs may also have low motivation to gather information about food items.
Pet dogs often need to locate food in their environment, and perhaps as a result they are skilled at tasks requiring locating a food item.
However, evaluating and then choosing between two items may be a much less frequently encountered task in their everyday environment, and may therefore be less ecologically relevant.

This may be because there is little pressure on pet dogs to make optimal choices between food items (i.e., only missing an opportunity to eat the preferred food), or the selection of the non-preferred item could reflect dogs' lack of understanding about the first-touch rule.

Studies 1 and 2 demonstrated that both in-lab and over Zoom, dogs prefer high value to low value foods, that familiarity with the items does not have a significant impact, and that preferences expressed through choices are comparatively weak, with dogs choosing the higher value item approximately 60% of the time across Studies 1 and 2.

It's possible that dogs' performance on food choice tasks is limited by the choice context itself -namely that due to social, experiential, procedural (i.e., low cost of choosing the less-preferred item) factors, dogs have a difficult time choosing between two food items.
As a result, we created a revised version of a forced-choice task.
Dogs were presented with two plates, each of which contained several high or low quality familiar food items (rather than an individual item).
One plate was always placed significantly closer to the dog, and the other a farther distance away.

If dogs have a strong preference for the high quality item then we would predict that when the plate with low quality items is closer to the dog, they will leave most if not all of the items on the plate, in order to quickly begin eating from the far plate (which contains the high quality items).
Alternatively, when the high quality plate is closer to the dog, we predict that dogs will leave few if any items on the closer plate, before moving on to the low quality items on the far plate.

It is also possible that dogs will not display a strong preference for the high quality item, in which case we would predict they will leave few if any items on the close plate before proceeding to the far plate, regardless of what food items are on that plate.

Though less likely, dogs could instead have a preference for the far plate, in which case we would predict that they would leave many or all items on the close plate regardless of what food items are on that plate.

By allowing dogs the opportunity to switch to an alternative choice and providing dogs with additional information before their choice (specifically by allowing them to look closely at, smell, and even taste both options) we aim to address possible challenges of twoalternative forced-choice tasks that may have resulted in past weak preferences.

text.text: Study 3 Experimental Set Up.
We conducted warm-up trials to ensure dogs were comfortable taking food off of a plate from both locations, and to give dog guardians a chance to practice the procedure.
Once the dog was in place behind marker 1, the guardian-experimenter showed one piece of a warm-up food (a food their dog would find rewarding that was not either the high or low quality food).
The guardian then allowed their dog to sniff the food by holding the plate a maximum of six inches from the dogs' nose.
This ensured that dogs had both visual and olfactory information about the contents of the plate.
Guardians then placed the plate on either Marker 2 or 3 (order counterbalanced), and walked behind their dog.
This ensured that, at the time of their choice, dogs were not able to see their guardians.
Once behind their dog, the guardian experimenter provided a verbal release, and the dog was allowed to approach and consume the warm-up food.
This process was repeated twice so the dog had the chance to eat the warm-up food at both Marker 2 and 3.
As a final step in warmups, guardians handed their dog a piece of each test food and verified the dog would eat it.
All dogs completed two test trials comparing the high and low quality items.
On one trial, the high quality item was closer to the dogs, and on the other the low quality item was closer.
The order of trials was counterbalanced across dogs.
To begin a trial, the guardian spread 8 pieces of the food items onto each plate.
This ensured dogs could not consume all food pieces in one bite.

With the dog ready at Marker 1, the guardian experimenter would show their dog the plate containing either the high or low quality food items and allow their dog to sniff the contents, as in the warm-up trials.
The order of presentation was counterbalanced, and was conducted in the same manner as the warm-up trials.
A trial ended either after the dog consumed all foods present, or after 30 seconds had elapsed since the dog stopped eating.
As in Study 1, the video experimenter live coded all trials, recording the first plate the dog touched, first ate from, and the first plate they finished (meaning all food items had been consumed).
In addition, the experimenter recorded the number of food items left on the closer plate at the time that the first item was eaten from the far plate.

An additional coder who was blind to the purpose of the study and the study's hypotheses also coded for each of these measures on 25% of the videos (n = 9 dogs) to ensure the data was recorded correctly.
Initial re-coded reliability was very high across our measures (97.22%).
As in Study 2, when disagreements between the experimenter and the naive coder occurred, the co-first-author (MHP) re-coded the trial.
All statistical analyses were conducted in R (v4.5.3; R Core Team, 2026), scripts and data available on OSF following publication.

We conducted a series of mixed-effects logistic regressions predicting dogs first touch, first eaten from, and first plate finished (close vs. far) as a function of the item on that plate with a random effect per dog.
For analyses involving first plate finished, we excluded dogs who did not finish either plate.
A total of 3 dogs were excluded from these analyses.

Finally, we examined whether the number of items left on the close plate at Marker 2, at the time when the food was first consumed from the far plate (Marker 3), was predicted by the contents of the close plate.
We used a mixed effect model to explore the number of items left as a function of the quality (high or low) of the items on the close plate with a random effect of dog.
Dogs tended to first touch the closer plate (chosen on 65 / 72 total trials); however, this did vary by what was on the closer plate.
When the high quality item was close, dogs touched that one first on 35 / 36 trials, whereas when the low quality item was close, dogs touched the low quality item first on 30 / 36 trials.
We found a significant effect of block, or that their first touch was different as a function of the contents of the closer plate, χ 2 (1) = 5.27, p = .02.
Similarly, dogs tended to first eat the closer plate (chose on 61 / 72 total trials), and this varied by what was on the closer plate.
There were only 4 trials where dogs first touched the closer plate but first ate from the further one.

When the high quality item was close, dogs first ate from the high quality item on 35 / 36 trials, whereas when the low quality item was close, dogs chose the low quality item first on 26 / 36 trials.
As in first touch, we found a significant effect of block with dogs first eating from the closer plate more when it contained the high quality item, χ 2 (1) = 6.22, p = .01.

On those trials, every dog ate all the high quality pieces.
When the high quality item was far away, one dog left all the high quality items uneaten (and consumed all the close low quality items), and another dog left all the low quality items uneaten.

Overall, these results support that dogs show a preference for food items based on their quality, and suggest that classic two alternative forced choice tasks may underestimate relatively robust item preferences in dogs, which may emerge more clearly when the task demands are reduced and sequential sampling of the food items is allowed.
Across three studies we examined dogs' food preferences in-lab (Study 1) and using a synchronous citizen science approach (Studies 2 and 3).
In Study 1, we used four task variations of a classic, two-alternative forced choice task in a laboratory setting.

We manipulated the presentation of the items and found that when presented with direct comparisons between a high quality item and a low quality item, dogs preferred the high quality item, but chose it at rates only slightly above chance (~60%).
In Study 2, we explored the impact of both item quality and familiarity on dogs' food preferences using a Zoom set-up with guardians acting as experimenters.
When evaluating preferences, we found that the quality of the food, and not its familiarity, drives dogs' food choices.
Dogs preferred higher quality items relative to lower quality items, choosing the higher quality item significantly more often, though still only (~60% of the time, as in Study 1).
We also found that when choosing foods relative familiarity does not play a significant role.
Dogs were neither neophobic nor neophilic when choosing between food items.

Put another way, in a twoalternative forced choice task dogs choose foods based on their quality alone, choosing the higher quality item no matter how familiar it was to them, or how familiar the alternative was.
As in Study 1, we found that while as a group dogs chose the higher quality food item significantly more often, few dogs individually displayed strong preferences, as measured by choice behavior.

In Study 3, we introduced a novel alternative to the two-alternative forced-choice task by presenting high-and low-quality foods on separate plates that dogs could approach sequentially, enabling more naturalistic measures of first contact, amount consumed, and switching between plates.
We found further evidence that dogs do prefer high quality to low quality items.
Dogs were more likely to first touch, eat from, and consume the entirety of the high quality plate, relative to the low quality plate.
Dogs also left significantly more food items behind when the close item was low quality, relative to high quality.
This evidence of food-related preferences is more apparent when we used a methodological variation compared to Studies 1 & 2 and considered additional indicators of preference.

text.text: While all methods in the present paper are iterations of the two-alternative forced choice paradigm, perhaps measuring behaviors other than first-touch (e.g., consumption) is an important additional finding; it raises the broader question of whether first-touch as a response is an accurate, species appropriate, method for understanding dog preferences.

Put another way, when the closer item was low quality dogs were more likely to leave the plate unfinished and move on to the far away high quality item, as compared to when the closer item was high quality.
Our findings are in line with previous work that dogs form strong preferences for food items (Cameron et al., 2021; Vicars et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Our findings are in line with previous work that dogs form strong preferences for food items <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Cameron et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Vicars et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: In the current Studies 2 and 3, dogs as a group preferred to eat the higher quality item over a lower quality item, regardless of how novel the items were.

In a similar vein, when dogs have been tested in paradigms that required greater effort to obtain a high quality reward, dogs would consistently work harder to receive a preferred item over a non-preferred item (Riemer et al., 2018), even when greater quantities of the non-preferred were available.

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that there are reliable preferences for food items underlying dog choice behavior and that this outweighs the importance of exploring new or greater aggregates of items.
Interestingly, even though dogs form strong preferences and can act on them to make choices, these preferences were only weakly reflected in their choices in Studies 1 and 2.
Instead, choice behavior appears to be highly variable.
One explanation for inconsistent choices across tasks is that different experimental set-ups have different cognitive demands, which may impact impulsive behavior.

Prior work has examined dogs' executive function in various paradigms from physical detours (e.g., Bray et al., 2014), adapted delay of gratification tasks (Brucks et al., 2017), and in personality assessments of impulsivity as a general factor underlying behavior (Riemer et al., 2014; Barela et al., 2024).

text.text: Across these studies there is general consensus that choice behavior varies greatly by individual, and that there is low transfer across contexts.

In Study 1 of this investigation, dogs displayed a marked preference for hot dogs over corn kernels in their consumption, sometimes spitting out the corn, but chose the higher quality item only modestly above chance.
This could point to potential distracting features of the experimental set up that made it more challenging for dogs to inhibit motor impulsivity and select the higher quality option.
For example, in Study 1, equalizing odor cues with the hotdog scent everywhere was an effective control, but also could have contributed to the decision-making difficulty.
It would have ensured that the high quality item was not more salient, however it could have sent a very strong signal that would have been difficult for dogs to ignore in favor of visual cues.
These results highlight the need for tasks that decouple what dogs value from their decision making, particularly under different cognitive loads.

Future work could consider exploring food preferences in a different dog population, such as free-ranging dogs, where there may be greater pressures to obtain better foods, and where novel foods may present both greater risks and benefits.
Further, all dogs in our sample are pets being presented with food items by a human.
In Studies 2 and 3, having the guardian act as an experimenter in the home was advantageous as it allowed us to customize food choices for individual dogs.
However, social expectations and past reward history with their guardian may have impacted dogs' performance.

While in Study 3 we had guardians move out of view of their dog to minimize any social cues or expectations at the time of choice, the presentation of the foods themselves was social across our three studies and could have impacted dogs' performance.
Future work could consider an entirely a-social version of this task to determine if dogs display stronger preference through choice behavior without the presence of a human.
In all, we found dogs prefer to eat higher quality vs. lower quality items but did not consistently choose the higher quality item first in variations of two-alternative choice tasks.

Dogs displayed this preference for higher (vs. lower) quality foods across two contexts: both under standardized conditions in the lab and in the home where food items could be tailored to individuals' preferred food types.

Surprisingly, though dogs are often characterized as neophilic (Kaulfuss & Mills, 2008), the novelty of items (which we operationalized as familiarity) does not appear to play a strong role in dogs' food choices, suggesting that dogs are neither neophobic nor neophilic when choosing food items.

text.text: Across studies, we observed a disconnect in which food dogs preferred to eat and which was chosen first, suggesting that some choice paradigms may not accurately capture preferences.
These results have an impact on future canine science studies and experimental design, as well as dog training.
Finally, this helps us to better understand how dogs make decisions and form preferences about the items in their environment.

For Studies 2 and 3, using a synchronous citizen science approach, we prepared instructions for the guardian to learn and perform the experimental procedure in their homes with live support from a researcher on zoom.
In a follow-up analysis, as a secondary measure of their preferences, we examined whether or not dogs ate the chosen item on each trial.
Using videos of the test sessions, we coded the outcome of each trial as "ate" the item (1) or "did not eat" the item (0).
To be coded as "ate", the dog needed to have consumed the entire available item.
Items that were left on the plate, licked, or taken in the mouth then spat out were coded as "did not eat."

We applied a generalized linear mixed-effects model with a binomial distribution and logit link function (lme4 library in R) to examine whether the value of the item predicted eating or not after choice.
Trials were nested within dog via a random intercept.
We found a significant association between choosing the high (vs. low) value item and the probability of consuming the item, b = 6.34, SE = 0.66, z = 9.67, p < .001.
